docs.title: UiPath Coding Agents Workshop
docs.text:
Build UiPath agents and Maestro orchestrations with coding agents — from installing the tools to shipping a long-running automation.

Training Environment

Log in at https://cloud.uipath.com/tpenlabs using tenant CodingAgentsPractice.

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text:
This workshop takes you from zero to building real automation with coding agents. You start by setting up the uip CLI and UiPath skills, then build agents and orchestrations — letting a coding agent like Claude Code do the heavy lifting while you stay in control.

The course has two parts:

Part 1 · Coding Agents — get your environment ready, learn how building UiPath components changes with a coding agent, and build your first agents: a low-code hello-world, a coded agent with context and tools, and a conversational agent.

Part 2 · Agentic Orchestration — build Coded Apps, then orchestrate agents and apps into Maestro solutions: Case Management, BPMN, and Flow.

Getting Started with Coding Agents — Install the uip CLI and UiPath skills, explore the CLI, then build and publish your first agent with Claude Code.

Loan Application Underwriting — Build a complete code-first underwriting pipeline: a Python coded agent, a React coded app, a Maestro flow, and an RPA workflow that assess and route loan applications for UiBank.

More exercises are being authored and will appear here as they are released.

docs.title: Key concepts
docs.text:
• Coding agent — an AI assistant (e.g., Claude Code) that builds UiPath components from your instructions, using the uip CLI and UiPath skills. UiPath is the automation platform that coding agents operate natively.
  • uip CLI — the command-line interface coding agents use to talk to the UiPath platform.
  • UiPath skills — curated instruction packs that teach a coding agent how to build UiPath automations correctly.
  • Maestro — UiPath's orchestration platform for coordinating humans, robots, and AI agents across long-running processes.

docs.title: Getting Started with Coding Agents
docs.text: Set up the UiPath CLI and skills, get a feel for the CLI, then build and publish your first agent — all from your coding agent.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A coding agent can build and operate UiPath automations the same way a developer does, once it knows how. You teach it with two things:

  • UiPath CLI, the command-line interface agents use to talk to the platform
  • UiPath Skills, curated instruction packs that tell the agent when and how to use that CLI

This first exercise is your preparation. You'll get your environment ready, get a feel for the CLI/Skills capabilities and usage, and then run the full build-and-publish loop once with a small agent — describe it to your coding agent, watch it scaffold, push it to Studio Web, and run it. The agent is intentionally simple; the point is to learn the workflow you'll reuse for every (richer) agent in the exercises that follow.

Before you begin: prerequisites

Have these ready before the session. The one thing to set up in advance is a coding agent:

  • A coding agent installed and signed in — Currently skills are available for: Claude Code, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI, Codex, OpenCode. Pick and install it and log in ahead of time; everything else, the agent can help you set up live. You'll also need a valid subscription or API key to interact with LLMs.
  • A laptop you can install software on (you usually need admin rights for installers).
  • A UiPath Cloud account. In this workshop we will use: https://cloud.uipath.com/tpenlabs/CodingAgentsPractice. Talk to your trainer if you are not invited.
  • Node.js / npm — needed for the UiPath CLI. If it's missing, your coding agent can install it for you.
  • Reliable internet, and a VPN if your company requires one.

You'll install the UiPath CLI and skills in first lesson, no need to do that beforehand.

Step Focus Install the CLI and Skills Install uip, authenticate, and add the UiPath skills to your coding agent Practice the CLI Explore the CLI, read from the platform, ask the docs with docsai, and send feedback Build Your First Agent Generate a simple low-code agent with Claude Code, then publish it to Studio Web, run it against sample claims, and review the result

Training Environment

Log in at https://cloud.uipath.com/tpenlabs using tenant CodingAgentsPractice.

docs.title: Installing the CLI and Skills
docs.text:
Here is our plan for this lesson:

  1. Install the UiPath CLI and sign in.
  2. Add the UiPath skills to your coding agent.
  3. Verify that your agent recognizes UiPath tasks.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: By the end of this lesson you'll have a working setup: the uip CLI installed and authenticated, the UiPath skills added, and a quick check that proves your agent knows how to build with UiPath. This is the foundation for every other exercise.

docs.title: Why a coding agent changes how you build
docs.text:
A coding agent already knows how to write code. What it doesn't know is UiPath — your CLI commands, project structures, and platform conventions. Two pieces fix that:

  • UiPath CLI is the interface the agent uses to talk to the platform. A command-line interface turned out to be the most token-efficient way to expose UiPath to an agent.
  • Skills are how you teach the agent to use that CLI well. They encode the sequence of commands for a task, so you can ask for an outcome instead of memorizing commands.

One idea worth holding onto: building is only a small part of the work. The agent gets you to a result quickly, but the platform is what keeps that result running, governed, and observable in production. You build at the edges; UiPath handles the infrastructure underneath.

docs.title: 1. Install the UiPath CLI
docs.text:
Install the CLI globally. This gives you the uip command.

npm install -g @uipath/cli

docs.title: 2. Sign in
docs.text:
Authenticate once. Your coding agent reuses this same session, so it acts as you on the platform.

uip login

docs.title: 3. Install the UiPath skills
docs.text:
uip skills install will launch an interactive installer for skills where you can pick your agent.

Add the skills for a specific agent, e.g. Claude Code:

uip skills install --agent claude

The installer walks you through selecting which skill bundles you need. For RPA pick uipath-rpa and uipath-platform. Add uipath-coded-workflows if you will also author coded workflows, and uipath-agents, uipath-maestro-flow if your project includes those.

Skills are published to GitHub, so you can pull them into custom toolchains and fork them for your own internal best practices.

Good to know

The skills registry is public, so this step needs no login. You also don't need to install platform tools first — your agent auto-installs them on first use. Claude Code is global-only for skills; the --local flag is for other agents like Cursor.

A few commands to keep handy:

Check your connection:

uip login status

Connect to a different environment:

uip login --authority https://staging.uipath.com -t <TenantName>

Check the version and keep tools current:

uip --version
uip tools update
uip skills update

uip --help and uip <command> --help are your best friends, right after your coding agent.

docs.title: 4. Verify the setup
docs.text:
To validate the currently installed tools, you can use the following commands:

uip --version
uip tools list --output table
uip skills list

Run your agent with new skills and then ask it for an outcome — not a command:

which uipath skills I can use? can you list tenants within environments I'm connected to?

A correctly set-up agent will use the tools and give you the answer. If it doesn't recognize UiPath tasks, restart Claude Code once more so it reloads plugins.

Sessions, identity, and security

The agent inherits your session and acts with your permissions. For a shared or service identity, sign in with an External Application session instead of a personal login.

Some agents run commands in isolated environments. In that case, they may not be able to run uip with your privileges. If uip login status shows you're connected in your terminal but your agent says otherwise, tell it:

When using the UiPath CLI, prefer escalated execution because sandboxed commands may not reflect my real terminal session

Avoid approving a blanket uip rule — that also covers destructive commands. Better to approve read/list prefixes as they come up.

Done. Your environment is ready.

docs.title: Practicing the CLI
docs.text:
Here is our plan for this lesson:

  1. Explore what the CLI can do.
  2. Read something from the platform.
  3. Ask the documentation a question with docsai.
  4. Send feedback without leaving your terminal.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Get comfortable with the uip CLI before you build with it. You'll run a few read-only commands, query the docs from the command line, and learn how to send feedback — so the CLI feels familiar when the agent starts driving it for you.

docs.title: Tools and skills
docs.text: Two extension systems sit beside the core CLI. Tools add commands that talk to UiPath services (Orchestrator, Integration Service, and so on). Skills teach your coding agent how to use those commands. You install both through the CLI, and during preview they update often — so pull the latest regularly.

docs.title: 1. See what's available
docs.text:
Start with the built-in help and the installed tools. The help is authoritative — when your agent gets stuck later, the fastest fix is to have it run --help and read the output.

uip --help
uip tools list --output table

docs.title: 2. Ask the docs with docsai
docs.text:
docsai answers UiPath questions from the terminal, grounded in the documentation.

uip docsai --help
uip docsai ask "How do I list Orchestrator folders with the UiPath CLI?"

docs.title: 3. Read from the platform
docs.text:
The docsai step likely surfaced this command — go ahead and run it:

uip or folders list

Let the agent drive

You rarely need to memorize these commands. The point of skills is that you ask for an outcome, for example "list the folders I can publish to", and the agent picks the right uip command. Running a few yourself builds intuition. In repeatable cases, scripted commands also save tokens compared to asking the agent each time.

docs.title: 4. Send feedback
docs.text:
Coding agents are still in a preview stage, so feedback matters. The easiest way is to ask your coding agent directly — there's a skill that packages the details and sends them to UiPath for you. If something went odd during a session, for example you see agent trying something in loops or retrying multiple times, ask your agent to describe it and use the feedback skill.

Send UiPath feedback: the docsai answer for X was incomplete because ...

If you note anything odd during session, for example CLI and skills mismatch or CLI doesn't work as expected, feel free to send that as feedback to UiPath using the send-feedback skill.

Done. You've used the CLI directly, queried the docs, and know how to report issues — everything you need before letting the agent build for you.

docs.title: Build, Test and Improve Your First Agent
docs.text:
Here is our plan for this lesson:

  1. Ask your coding agent to build a small agent from a prompt, then try it on a sample claim.
  2. Turn a few test documents into an evaluation set.
  3. Run the evaluations in a loop, letting your coding agent improve the agent.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
By the end of this lesson you'll have a working low-code agent in Studio Web and a set of tests that tell you whether the agent works. You'll also have run the loop you'll use for every agent after this one: describe it, build it, test it, fix it, test again.

The agent is deliberately small, so the focus stays on that loop. Later exercises build richer agents with context, tools and structured extraction.

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text:
An insurer receives a First Notice of Loss (FNOL) claim together with the homeowner's policy it refers to. Before anyone assesses the damage, someone checks the basics. We will build an agent to do that.

It reads both PDFs and runs five checks:

  1. Policy status: is the policy Current or Paid, rather than Lapsed, Cancelled or Expired?
  2. Identity: is the claimant the person named on the policy?
  3. Address: do the claim and the policy describe the same property?
  4. Coverage period: did the loss happen while the policy was in force?
  5. Filing deadline: was the claim filed within 60 days of the loss, or does it explain why not?

It returns a yes or no on eligibility, a flag for claims a person should look at, a short summary, and the result of each check as JSON. Other apps and agents could read that JSON, so the field names and output structure are fixed.

docs.title: Why test an agent at all?
docs.text:
An LLM doesn't always give the same answer twice. A prompt that works on the sample you tried can still trip on a date written as 10.10.2026, on a claimant who shares a surname with the policyholder, or on an explanation hidden in the middle of a paragraph. A small change to the prompt, or a new model, can break a case that used to pass.

An evaluation set run regularly catches that. It's a list of test cases of all business scenarios, each one an input plus the answer you expect. You run the whole set after every change and compare scores. The checks that do the scoring are called evaluators. You'll use three kinds:

Evaluator What it checks here Exact match The decision fields out_isEligible and out_Escalate are exactly right JSON similarity The five check results and the values behind them match LLM judge The summary gives the same decision and the same reason, in any LLM's wording / language / length, as long as it's valid

Writing good test cases is the hard part - we expect business users to provide samples. In this exercise a document generator does it for you: it creates a claim and a policy with one known problem planted in them, so you know what the right answer is.

Training Environment

Log in at https://cloud.uipath.com/tpenlabs and use tenant CodingAgentsPractice for this exercise.

docs.title: 1. Set up your working folder
docs.text:
Create an empty folder with a samples subfolder:

mkdir first-agent
cd first-agent
mkdir samples

Download the sample claim and its policy into samples:

Claim Policy Scenario CLM-2026-809765-claim.pdf HO-81987766.pdf Melbourne (AUD), fire damage, Mei Lin Tan

Open them. The dates are written day first, and the loss happened on the last day of the policy. Your agent will have to get both of those right.

Optional: define your conventions (AGENTS.md)

Before you build much, drop a small file in the folder with your conventions: naming, structure, and rules like "keep workflows small; don't put everything in one folder".

  • Your coding agent reads it automatically and follows it in every new session.
  • It steers the agent beyond a single prompt, which keeps the output consistent across sessions and across coding agents.
  • There's no single file name yet (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, GEMINI.md and so on). If you use several coding agents, keep one real file and symlink the others to it.
  • Here's a starting point. Expand it as you go:
# Creating new projects

- When I ask to build something in this workspace folder, create a new project folder (short, lowercase, hyphenated) instead of working in the workspace root.
- Initialize with `git init` unless already inside an existing repo.
- Add a project-level `AGENTS.md` (like this one) before substantial implementation, so future sessions keep the same behavior.
- Continue all implementation, validation, and file edits inside the new project folder.

# UiPath projects

- If a request mentions UiPath, RPA, Orchestrator, Maestro, Studio Web, `.xaml`, `.flow`, `.bpmn`, context grounding, queues, assets, robots, jobs, triggers, or `uip`, use the installed UiPath agent skills when relevant.
- Prefer the uip CLI for setup, validation, build, packaging, run, and platform operations.
- Ask before publishing, deploying, deleting, or modifying any UiPath Cloud/Orchestrator resource (package, folder, queue item, etc).

docs.title: 2. Build the agent
docs.text:
Open Claude Code (or your coding agent) in the first-agent folder and give it this prompt:

Using the UiPath agent skill, build a low-code agent called "EligibilityCheckAgent" in a solution called "EligibilityCheck" followed by my first or last name. The agent takes two PDF files, a claim and a policy, reads both, and checks the claim against the policy.

Inputs:
- in_ClaimPDF: the First Notice of Loss (FNOL) claim form submitted by the claimant (PDF).
- in_PolicyPDF: the homeowner's insurance policy referenced by the claim (PDF).

Things the agent needs to check between the two documents:
1. Policy Status Check. Find the Payment Status on the policy. Acceptable statuses are "Current"
   and "Paid". If it is "Lapsed", "Cancelled", or "Expired", the check fails.
2. Identity Verification. Compare the Claimant Name on the claim to the Named Insured on the
   policy. Allow minor variations (nicknames, middle names, minor spelling). If they refer to
   different people, the check fails.
3. Property Address Match. Compare the property address on the claim and the policy. Normalize
   formatting (e.g. "St." vs "Street"). If they differ, the check fails. This exercise has no
   separate incident report, so set report_address to "N/A — no incident report in this exercise".
4. Coverage Period Check. Confirm the Incident Date falls on or after the policy Effective Date
   and on or before the Expiration Date. A loss on the first or last day passes. If outside this
   window, the check fails.
5. Filing Deadline Check. Calculate calendar days between the Incident Date and the Date of
   Submission. More than 60 days: check whether the claim gives an explicit explanation for the delay.
   Explanation → pass (and escalate, see below). No explanation → fail. The form's pre-printed
   60-day notice is not an explanation.

The agent must return output matching this structure. Downstream apps and agents depend on it:
{
  "out_isEligible": "boolean: whether the claim is eligible for assessment",
  "out_EligibilityAnalysisSummary": "string: brief plain-language explanation of the decision",
  "out_Escalate": "boolean: true if a person needs to look at the claim (late filing with an explanation, or a document that can't be read)",
  "out_EligibilityChecksJSON": {
    "claim_id": "string",
    "policy_number": "string",
    "checks": {
      "policy_status": {
        "result": "pass | fail",
        "summary": "string"
      },
      "identity_match": {
        "result": "pass | fail",
        "claimant_name": "string",
        "policyholder_name": "string",
        "summary": "string"
      },
      "address_match": {
        "result": "pass | fail",
        "claim_address": "string",
        "policy_address": "string",
        "report_address": "string",
        "summary": "string"
      },
      "coverage_period": {
        "result": "pass | fail",
        "incident_date": "string",
        "effective_date": "string",
        "expiration_date": "string",
        "summary": "string"
      },
      "filing_deadline": {
        "result": "pass | fail",
        "incident_date": "string",
        "claim_date": "string",
        "days_elapsed": "number",
        "summary": "string"
      }
    }
  }
}

- All checks pass → out_isEligible = true, otherwise false.
- Late filing with an explanation → out_isEligible = true, out_Escalate = true.
- The agent should not infer information that isn't explicitly in the documents.
- This is the FNOL eligibility step for property claims. Write the prompt with common practice in
  this area in mind. That can guide how values are read and normalized, but must not add checks,
  escalation reasons or pass/fail rules beyond the ones above.
- The decision must follow from the checks. In the output schema, put out_EligibilityChecksJSON
  first and out_isEligible, out_Escalate and out_EligibilityAnalysisSummary after it; inside each
  check, put the details first and result last. Keep the field names and types. The summary must
  agree with the check results.
- Every output field always gets a value of the right type, even when a document can't be read.
  In that case the checks fail and out_Escalate = true.
- The prompt should be well structured and easy for a person to read.

There's a sample claim and its policy in the samples folder. When the agent is built, upload it to Studio Web and try it on the sample. Don't deploy it.

Approve the steps if agent asks. In our test runs this took about four minutes, and the coding agent worked through roughly this sequence:

  • read the UiPath agent skill and the sample PDFs;
  • create the solution and the agent inside it; local first;
  • write the agent's system prompt, the two file inputs and the output schema, and add the built-in Analyze Files tool, which is how a low-code agent reads a PDF;
  • validate the project, upload it to Studio Web, and run the agent once on a sample pair.

Open the agent in Studio Web to see what the coding agent built: the two file inputs, the output schema, the system and user prompts, and the Analyze Files tool on the canvas.

Here is the output from one of our runs on the sample (claim CLM-2026-809765)

Exact wording will vary

The summaries are generated, so yours won't match ours word for word. The structure, each check's result and the decision should match. Nothing is wrong with the sample claim, so it should come back out_isEligible: true and out_Escalate: false. The claims with problems come in step 4.

Field names in the terminal

When the coding agent runs the agent from the CLI, the output it prints may show the field names in PascalCase (OutIsEligible, ClaimId). That's only how the CLI displays them. The agent's real output uses the names from your schema.

docs.title: 3. Test the agent by hand
docs.text:
1. Open the solution your coding agent uploaded in Studio Web. It's called EligibilityCheck followed by your name. The coding agent also shows the Studio Web project URL.
  2. Open EligibilityCheckAgent and select Debug.
  3. Set in_ClaimPDF and in_PolicyPDF to the sample claim and its policy, and run it.
  4. Look at the output and validate that all arguments and JSON payload structure is correct.
  5. When the run finishes, add it to the Default Evaluation Set.

docs.title: 4. Create the evaluation set
docs.text:
You need seven test cases: one clean claim, one for each check that can fail, and one late claim that explains the delay, which a person should review.

Choose the tab that matches your setup. Both give you the same evaluation set.

Run the document generatorUse the offline kit

The Retrieve Property Claim process creates a claim and a policy with a planted problem and saves them to storage buckets. Give your coding agent this prompt:

Using the UiPath agent skill, create an evaluation set for the agent. An evaluation set is a list of test cases: input files plus the answer we expect. Create it and upload it to Studio Web, but don't run it yet.

To get test documents, run the process "Retrieve Property Claim" in the Orchestrator folder "ClaimCase-Pro" once per test case, setting only in_Scenario and in_Discrepancy. It returns the claim ID and saves the claim form as <ClaimID>-claim.pdf in the storage bucket "Claims" in the same folder. The matching policy is <PolicyNumber>.pdf in the bucket "Insurance Policies Repository".

Test cases (7, one per line):
- in_Scenario = auto-settle: nothing is wrong, so the claim is eligible
- in_Scenario = eligibility-fail, with in_Discrepancy =
  - ELIG_POLICY_LAPSED: premium unpaid from before the loss, so policy_status fails
  - ELIG_IDENTITY_MISMATCH: policy in a household member's name, so identity_match fails
  - ELIG_ADDRESS_MISMATCH: the house or unit number differs, so address_match fails
  - ELIG_COVERAGE_PERIOD: policy ended 5–20 days before the loss, so coverage_period fails
  - ELIG_LATE_FILING: loss 75–90 days before filing, no explanation, so filing_deadline fails
- in_Scenario = review-fail, with in_Discrepancy = REVIEW_LATE_WITH_JUSTIFICATION: filed late,
  but the claim explains why, so the claim is eligible and escalated
Name each test case after its setting, e.g. "ELIG_LATE_FILING". Call the first one "AUTO_SETTLE".

Work out the expected answers from the PDFs.

How to score each test case:
1) Exact match on out_isEligible and out_Escalate: is the decision right?
2) JSON similarity on out_EligibilityChecksJSON: are the check results and values right? Compare
   only the results and values, not the wording of the summaries.
3) LLM judge on out_EligibilityAnalysisSummary: does the summary give the same decision and reason?
   Use a different model for the judge than the agent uses.

Until the UiPath skill covers this, here's how evaluation files work. Studio Web keeps them in the agent's evaluationFiles folder as text, not as plain PDFs: the first line is BINARY_FILE:application/pdf:<size>, the next line is ---BASE64---, and then comes the PDF as base64. Files you download from Studio Web are already in that format. Test cases point at them as evaluationFiles/<name>.pdf, like the test case I added in Studio Web.

Put everything in a new evaluation set called "Eligibility Scenarios". Don't change or delete other evaluation sets.

I'm editing in Studio Web in parallel, so merge with my version before uploading.

The documents are generated fresh each time, so your claims, names and dates will differ from everyone else's.

No access to the generator? Download eval-documents.zip and unzip it into an eval-documents folder next to samples. It holds seven claim and policy pairs produced by the same generator, plus cases.csv, which says which claim goes with which policy and what's wrong with each pair. The test documents are in the eval-documents folder. cases.csv lists the 7 test cases: which claim and policy go together, and what's wrong with each one. Use one test case per row and name it after the case column, e.g. "ELIG_LATE_FILING".

2) JSON similarity on out_EligibilityChecksJSON: are the check results and values right? Compare

Files you download from Studio Web are already in that format. Test cases point at them as evaluationFiles/<name>.pdf, like the test case I added in Studio Web.

Put everything in a new evaluation set called "Eligibility Scenarios". Don't change or delete other evaluation sets.

I'm editing in Studio Web in parallel, so merge with my version before uploading.

You just edited the solution in Studio Web, so the last line of the prompt tells the coding agent to download your version first and keep your test case. In our runs it compared the two copies, kept the Studio Web changes, and checked again right before uploading.

When it's done, open Eligibility Scenarios in Studio Web. You should see seven test cases, each with a claim and a policy attached. Check a couple of expected answers against the PDFs yourself: the coding agent worked them out by reading the documents, and so can you.

Seven test cases, one per scenario. For AUTO_SETTLE the expected output says eligible and no escalation.

The Evaluators tab shows how each test case gets scored. Each evaluator looks at one output field: the two decisions get an exact match, the checks get JSON similarity, and the summary gets an LLM judge.

docs.title: 5. Test and fix
docs.text:
Now the loop. Give your coding agent this prompt:

Next, I want to make sure the agent's prompt works on all known test cases. Run the evaluation yourself from the CLI and see which test cases fail. If one fails, find out why, fix the prompt and run again. Repeat until the decisions are right on every case, the summary scores 95 or more and the JSON similarity 80 or more. Call it done only after two clean runs in a row. At most 3 fix iterations.

Until UiPath fixes it, runs started from the CLI can't open the evaluationFiles paths. For CLI runs, upload the test PDFs as attachments and run from a copy of the project whose test cases use those attachment IDs instead. Keep the agent's project ID the same as in Studio Web, and pass the solution ID. Leave the Studio Web evaluation set as it is.

Rules
- Improve the agent, not the test. Only change an expected answer if it's clearly wrong, and ask me first.
- Fix it with general rules, not with details from the test files.
- Look at every test case. A case that didn't run counts as failed.
- If the judge itself errors, rerun it; don't change the agent for that.
- Don't change the output format: same field names and types, because other apps depend on them.
- While you debug, don't change the model or add other evaluation sets. Ask me first.
- Don't deploy to Orchestrator.

At the end, show me
- a before-and-after table of scores
- each prompt change and the problem it fixed

The coding agent runs the whole loop itself: it starts each evaluation run from the CLI, reads the scores, changes the agent's prompt, uploads it and runs again. A run takes about a minute.

Every run, including the ones the coding agent starts from the CLI, lands on the Results tab of the evaluation set in Studio Web, newest at the top, with one score per evaluator. You can watch the scores climb as the coding agent fixes the prompt.

Why the prompt explains attachments

Right now, evaluation runs started from the CLI can't open files referenced as evaluationFiles/..., and every test case fails with INVALID_ATTACHMENT_ID. Runs started in Studio Web don't have this problem. Until UiPath fixes it, the prompt tells the coding agent how to work around it, so it can run the loop on its own.

In one of our runs the first baseline looked fine. A second run of the same prompt missed the late claim with an explanation: the agent said it wasn't eligible. The PDF explains the delay in the third person, in the middle of the incident description ("The claim is late because the claimant was admitted to hospital the day after the loss..."). The agent's prompt told it to look for an explanation "written by the claimant", and the model sometimes read past it.

The coding agent fixed it with general rules: read every free-text field on the claim, and count an explanation wherever it appears, in first or third person. After that fix:

Evaluator Baseline (run 1 / run 2) After the fix Target out_isEligible exact match 100 / 85.7 100 100 out_Escalate exact match 100 / 85.7 100 100 JSON similarity 99.98 / 98.3 99.98 80 Summary LLM judge 83.6 / 83.0 99.86 95

The low judge scores in the baseline aren't all the agent's fault. The judge model crashed on one case per run and scored it 0, which is why the prompt says to rerun when the judge itself errors, and why the judge uses a different model from the agent.

Notice that one passing run didn't settle it. The late claim passed once, failed once, then passed after the fix. That's why the prompt asks for two clean runs in a row.

docs.title: 6. Optional: try another model
docs.text:
How much does the result depend on the model? Ask your coding agent:

Now change the agent's model to gpt-5.6-luna, run the evaluation once, and show the scores next to the previous run. If any case fails, tell me why.

In our run, four of the seven cases failed outright: the new model left out three of the four output fields, so Studio Web rejected the output. The three cases that did run got the decisions right.

The run's overall scores hide this. They still read 100 for both decisions, 99.4 for JSON similarity and 97 for the summary, because the averages only count the cases that finished. Always read the scores per test case, not just the summary line.

Afterwards, ask your coding agent to switch the model back to Claude Sonnet 5.

Done. You built an agent with a coding agent, gave it a set of tests, and used those tests to find and fix a real problem.

docs.title: Claims Eligibility Agent — Prompt (Hello-World version)
docs.text: Self-contained version that reads the raw claim PDF and policy PDF directly. (Later in the course, an IXP-based version replaces raw-PDF reading with structured, validated extraction — the validation logic and output stay the same.)

docs.title: Role
docs.text: You are a Claims Eligibility Specialist. Your sole responsibility is to verify that a property insurance claim meets the threshold requirements for processing. You do not evaluate coverage, calculate payouts, or assess credibility. You only determine whether the claim is eligible to be reviewed.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
• in_ClaimPDF — the First Notice of Loss (FNOL) claim form submitted by the claimant (PDF).
  • in_PolicyPDF — the homeowner's insurance policy referenced by the claim (PDF).

Read both PDFs directly to find the values each check needs.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
Perform the following checks in order. If any check fails, stop and report the failure. Do not continue to subsequent checks after a hard failure.

  1. Policy Status Check. Find the Payment Status on the policy. Acceptable statuses are "Current" and "Paid". If it is "Lapsed", "Cancelled", or "Expired", the check fails.
  2. Identity Verification. Compare the Claimant Name on the claim to the Named Insured on the policy. Allow minor variations (nicknames, middle names, minor spelling). If they refer to different people, the check fails.
  3. Property Address Match. Compare the property address on the claim and the policy. Normalize formatting (e.g. "St." vs "Street"). If they differ, the check fails. (This exercise has no separate incident report, so set report_address to "N/A — no incident report in this exercise".)
  4. Coverage Period Check. Confirm the Incident Date falls on or after the policy Effective Date and on or before the Expiration Date. If outside this window, the check fails.
  5. Filing Deadline Check. Calculate calendar days between the Incident Date and the Date of Submission. If greater than 60 days, check whether the claim provides any explanation for the delay. No explanation → fail. Explanation present → flag as "late_with_justification" rather than a hard fail.

docs.title: Special Rules
docs.text:
• All checks pass → eligible = true, recommendation = "proceed_to_coverage_analysis".
  • Any hard fail → eligible = false, stop checking, recommendation = "deny".
  • Only issue is a late filing with justification → eligible = true, recommendation = "escalate".
  • Do not infer information that is not explicitly present in the documents.

docs.title: User prompt
docs.text: Check eligibility for the attached claim (in_ClaimPDF) against the attached policy (in_PolicyPDF).

docs.title: Loan Application Underwriting (Studio RPA, Coded Agent, Coded App, Maestro)
docs.text: Use the UiPath coding skills to build a complete code-first underwriting pipeline for UiBank

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
UiBank receives loan applications every day. Each one needs a credit assessment — income check, spending analysis, debt-to-income ratio — before a loan officer can make a decision. Doing this manually takes time, introduces inconsistency, and doesn't scale.

This exercise takes a code-first approach to the problem. Instead of configuring low-code workflows, you describe what you want to build in plain English — and your coding agent, equipped with UiPath skills, generates each component for you. You'll see exactly when code beats drag-and-drop, and why.

You'll build four components in this order: the coded agent first, then the loan officer app, then the Maestro flow that wires them together, and finally the RPA workflow that drives the whole process. Each lesson is self-contained — by the end, they all run together.

The use case: a CSV of loan applicants is processed row by row. For each applicant, the RPA submits a loan application to the UiBank API and immediately starts a Maestro process with the returned loan ID. Maestro runs the AI credit assessment, routes low-risk applications to an automatic approval, and sends medium and high-risk ones to a loan officer for review.

docs.title: What You'll Build
docs.text:
Four components, built in this order:

  1. Coded Agent — a Python LangGraph agent that receives a loan_id, calls the UiBank API to verify the quote and retrieve market data, computes financial metrics, and uses the LLM to produce a credit score, risk band, and assessment summary
  2. Loan Officer App — a React Coded Action App that presents the AI assessment to a loan officer and captures an Approve or Reject decision
  3. Maestro Flow — a UiPath Flow process that calls the agent, auto-approves low-risk results, and opens the loan officer app for medium and high-risk cases
  4. RPA Workflow — a Studio XAML workflow that reads loan-applications.csv, submits each row to the UiBank API, and starts the Maestro Flow process for each accepted application
📄 loan-applications.csv ↓ Studio RPA · LoanApplicationDispatcher For each row: POST /api/quotes/newquote → UiBank API uipath-rpa ↓ ◇  accepted == True? No write "Failed" to results.csv Yes start Maestro Flow with loan_id ↓ Maestro Flow · LoanUnderwritingProcess uipath-maestro-flow Coded Agent · LoanUnderwritingAgent Calls 3 UiBank API tools → returns risk_band · credit_score · assessment_summary uipath-agents ◇  risk_band == "Low"? Yes ✓ Auto-Approved No (Medium / High) Coded App · loan-officer-dashboard Loan officer reviews and submits decision uipath-coded-apps ◇  officer_decision == "Approve"? Yes ✓ Approved No ✗ Rejected ↓ RPA · write results to results.csv → upload to LoanUnderwriting storage bucket

docs.title: AI Underwriting Assessment
docs.text: Use the uipath-agents skill to generate a Python LangGraph agent that retrieves loan data from the UiBank API, computes financial metrics, and uses the LLM to interpret the results and produce a credit assessment.

docs.title: 1. Open Your Project Folder in Your Coding Agent
docs.text:
Create an empty folder called LoanUnderwritingAgent and open it in your coding agent (e.g. Claude Code, Codex):

mkdir LoanUnderwritingAgent

docs.title: 2. Describe the Agent
docs.text:
Give your coding agent a plain-English description of what to build:

Build a UiPath Coded Agent in LangGraph that:

1. Takes a loan_id as input
2. Verifies the loan quote by calling the UiBank API (https://uibank-api.uipath.com/explorer/swagger.json, no authentication required) and extracts the applicant's loan amount, loan term, yearly income, and age
3. Retrieves the average loan amount across all UiBank applications for market benchmarking
4. Computes raw financial metrics and surfaces them to the LLM: monthly repayment amount, debt-to-income ratio (the monthly repayment as a share of monthly income), and how the loan compares to the market average
5. Uses the LLM to interpret the metrics, assign a credit score (0–100) and risk band (Low / Medium / High), and generate a plain-English assessment summary

Include an eval set with 5 cases. The name of the agent should be {YourName}LoanUnderwritingAgent. Use the UiPath SDK.

Your coding agent reads the uipath-agents skill context and generates a complete agent project:

  • main.py — the agent entry point with the LangGraph graph definition (tools may be here or in a separate tools.py)
  • pyproject.toml — project configuration with uipath-langgraph dependency
  • evals/ — a folder with 5 evaluation cases

docs.title: 3. Review the Generated Code
docs.text:
Open the project in your IDE. Every coding agent generates slightly different code — the structure varies. What matters is that the essentials are there.

What to look for:

  • Three @tool-decorated functions — one each for verify_quote, get_average_loan_amount, and compute_financial_metrics. These may live in a separate tools.py or all inside main.py — either is fine.
  • A system prompt — a SYSTEM_PROMPT string instructing the LLM to interpret the financial metrics holistically and produce a credit score, risk band, and assessment summary. It's usually inline in main.py rather than a separate file — built as a plain prompt string.
  • An agent entry point — defined in langgraph.json, which points to main.py:graph (where graph = builder.compile()); this is also registered as the "agent" entry point in entry-points.json.
  • evals/ — 5 test cases covering a range of risk profiles, used to validate the agent's scoring behaviour with uipath eval.

Check the system prompt. It should instruct the LLM to reason about the combination of metrics and produce a natural language explanation — not map thresholds to a fixed score. If the prompt is too mechanical, ask your coding agent:

Update the system prompt so the LLM reasons about the combination of
factors rather than applying fixed rules — a high DTI with a small loan
amount should be treated differently from the same DTI with a large loan

docs.title: 2. Run and Verify Your Agent
docs.text:
Give this prompt to your coding agent — it finds real loan IDs across a spread of risk profiles, runs the agent against each, and checks the output:

1. Open and inspect the UiBank Swagger documentation:
   https://uibank-api.uipath.com/explorer/swagger.json

2. Using only documented, read-only endpoints, find 3 existing loan quotes
   that cover a spread of risk profiles — e.g. a small loan with a healthy
   income ratio, a large loan with a long term, and an applicant with a
   tight income-to-loan ratio.

   Requirements:
   - Do not create, update, or delete any data.
   - Do not invent or reuse an unverified loan_id — verify each record exists.

3. For each loan_id, run the coded agent, saving each result to its own output file.

4. Read each out-*.json and confirm it contains:
   - a credit_score between 0 and 100
   - a risk_band of Low, Medium, or High
   - a plain-English assessment summary that actually reasons about the
     metrics (debt-to-income ratio, market comparison) rather than generic text

5. Report a table: loan_id | loan amount | term | income | age | credit score | risk band.
   Flag anything suspicious — identical scores across very different profiles,
   missing fields, or an exception.

docs.text: Use the uipath-coded-apps skill to generate a React Coded Action App that renders inside Maestro's human task review — showing the AI credit assessment and letting the loan officer approve or reject the application.

docs.title: 2. Describe the App
docs.text:
Give your coding agent a plain-English description of what to build. Be specific about what the officer sees, where the data comes from, and what the decision buttons do:

Build a Coded Action App using UiPath TypeScript SDK called
{yourname}loanofficerdashboardApp. It should:

1. Receives twelve inputs: LoanId (string), ApplicantFirstName (string),
   ApplicantLastName (string), LoanAmount (number), LoanTerm (number),
   YearlyIncome (number) — passed from the Maestro process — and the six
   outputs of the coded agent: CreditScore (number, 0–100), RiskBand
   (string — Low / Medium / High), AssessmentSummary (string),
   MonthlyRepayment (number), DebtToIncomeRatio (number), and
   LoanToMarketRatio (number)
2. Display a two-panel dashboard: left panel shows the applicant name, LoanId,
   loan amount, loan term, and yearly income; right panel shows CreditScore as
   a progress bar, RiskBand as a colour-coded badge (green = Low, yellow =
   Medium, red = High), AssessmentSummary as a text block, and the three
   financial metrics (monthly repayment, debt-to-income ratio,
   loan-to-market ratio) as labelled values
3. Provide an optional Notes text area for the loan officer to add comments
4. Let the loan officer submit a decision via Approve (green) or Reject (red)
   buttons — defined as outcomes in action-schema.json, no external API calls
   needed

  • src/App.tsx — the main React component with the two-panel layout
  • action-schema.json — defines all inputs and the Approve/Reject outcomes
  • package.json — project dependencies

cd LoanOfficerDashboard

1. Receive six inputs: loan_id, applicant_first_name, applicant_last_name,
   loan_amount, loan_term, income
2. Call the agent {YourName}LoanUnderwritingAgent (in the CodingAgentsILT
   folder), passing loan_id and storing the returned values as process
   variables: credit_score, risk_band, assessment_summary,
   monthly_repayment, debt_to_income_ratio, loan_to_market_ratio
3. Auto-approve the application and end the process if risk_band is "Low"
4. For Medium or High risk, open the app {yourname}loanofficerdashboard (in the
   CodingAgentsILT folder), passing all twelve inputs: LoanId,
   ApplicantFirstName, ApplicantLastName, LoanAmount, LoanTerm, YearlyIncome,
   CreditScore, RiskBand, AssessmentSummary, MonthlyRepayment,
   DebtToIncomeRatio, LoanToMarketRatio — and capturing officer_decision
5. End with Approved or Rejected based on officer_decision
6. Output final_decision (string — "Approved" or "Rejected") in all cases,
   whether the application was auto-approved or decided by the loan officer

Your coding agent reads the uipath-maestro-flow skill context and generates a complete project:

  • {YourName}LoanUnderwritingProcess.flow — the flow definition with all nodes, edges, and variable mappings
  • project.uiproj — project manifest

docs.title: 3. Review the Generated Flow
docs.text:
Open {YourName}LoanUnderwritingProcess.flow in your text editor or ask your coding agent to describe the structure. You should see:

  • A Start node with six process input variables: loan_id, applicant_first_name, applicant_last_name, loan_amount, loan_term, income
  • An Agent node calling {YourName}LoanUnderwritingAgent with loan_id as input and six output variables: credit_score, risk_band, assessment_summary, monthly_repayment, debt_to_income_ratio, loan_to_market_ratio
  • A Condition node branching on risk_band == "Low"
  • A Human Task node wired to {yourname}loanofficerdashboard with all twelve variables mapped as inputs (LoanId, ApplicantFirstName, ApplicantLastName, LoanAmount, LoanTerm, YearlyIncome, CreditScore, RiskBand, AssessmentSummary, MonthlyRepayment, DebtToIncomeRatio, LoanToMarketRatio) and officer_decision as output
  • A second Condition node branching on officer_decision == "Approve"
  • Three End nodes — Auto-Approved, Approved, Rejected

If any mapping or condition needs adjusting, ask your coding agent:

Update the risk band condition so the default path goes to the human review
node and the explicit condition branch handles the "Low" auto-approve case

Visualise the flow in Studio Web

You can import the generated .flow file into Studio Web to see a visual diagram of the process and test it interactively — without deploying to Orchestrator first. Open Studio Web, create a new Flow project, and import {YourName}LoanUnderwritingProcess.flow. The canvas will render all nodes, conditions, and connections exactly as the coding agent generated them.

docs.title: 4. Test the Generated Flow
docs.text:
Ask your coding agent to fetch a verified loan record from UiBank and generate valid test input for the flow:

Open and inspect the UiBank Swagger documentation:

https://uibank-api.uipath.com/explorer/swagger.json

Using only endpoints documented by the API, identify the read-only endpoint for
retrieving loan quotes. Make a GET request and select one loan quote that
currently exists in UiBank.

Use the verified loan record to generate test input for the
{YourName}LoanUnderwritingProcess Flow.

Requirements:
- Use only GET endpoints documented in the Swagger specification.
- Do not create, update, or delete any data.
- Do not invent or reuse an unverified loan_id.
- Verify that the selected loan record exists.
- Populate loan_amount, loan_term, and income from the same verified record.
- loan_term represents years and must be one of: 1, 3, 5, or 10.
- Map the record's yearly income to income.
- Use applicant names from the record when available. If the API does not provide
  applicant names, use the workshop-safe values John and Doe.
- Return exactly one valid JSON object.
- Do not include Markdown, explanations, comments, or a PowerShell command.

Required output format:

{
  "loan_id": "<VERIFIED_LOAN_ID>",
  "applicant_first_name": "<FIRST_NAME>",
  "applicant_last_name": "<LAST_NAME>",
  "loan_amount": <LOAN_AMOUNT>,
  "loan_term": <1_OR_3_OR_5_OR_10>,
  "income": <YEARLY_INCOME>
}

Your coding agent should return something like:

{
  "loan_id": "6a4203a1f4865600481c657b",
  "applicant_first_name": "John",
  "applicant_last_name": "Doe",
  "loan_amount": 15000,
  "loan_term": 3,
  "income": 48000
}

docs.title: 5. Validate and Pack
docs.text:
ManuallyUsing Your Coding Agent

Navigate to the parent folder of the generated .flow file:

cd "parent-folder-path/to/{YourName}LoanUnderwritingProcess"

Replace the path with the actual location on your machine.

Validate the flow before packing:

uip maestro flow validate {YourName}LoanUnderwritingProcess.flow

If you get a command not found error, the maestro tool may not be installed or on your PATH:

# 1. Install maestro-tool (only needed once)
npm install -g @uipath/maestro-tool --prefix "$HOME/.npm-global"

# 2. Add it to PATH (needed each new terminal, or add to ~/.zshrc permanently)
export PATH="$HOME/.npm-global/bin:$PATH"

# To avoid step 2 every time, run this once:
echo 'export PATH="$HOME/.npm-global/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.zshrc

# 3. Validate
uip maestro flow validate {YourName}LoanUnderwritingProcess.flow

Fix any warnings, then pack:

uip maestro flow pack "<path-to-your-flow-folder>/{YourName}LoanUnderwritingProcess" /tmp/dist --version 1.0.0 --output json

For example:

uip maestro flow pack "/path/to/{YourName}LoanUnderwritingProcess/{YourName}LoanUnderwritingProcess" /tmp/dist --version 1.0.0 --output json

Upload the package to Orchestrator and create a process in the CodingAgentsILT folder:

uip or packages upload /tmp/dist/{YourName}LoanUnderwritingProcess.flow.Flow.1.0.0.nupkg --output json

For example:

uip or packages upload /tmp/dist/MadalinaLoanUnderwritingProcess.flow.Flow.1.0.0.nupkg --output json

If you get a command not found error, the maestro tool may not be installed or on your PATH:

# 1. Install maestro-tool (only needed once)
npm install -g @uipath/maestro-tool --prefix "$HOME/.npm-global"

# 2. Add it to PATH (needed each new terminal, or add to ~/.zshrc permanently)
export PATH="$HOME/.npm-global/bin:$PATH"

# To avoid step 2 every time, run this once:

# 3. Retry the upload

Then create the process:

uip or processes create --name "{YourName}LoanUnderwritingProcess" --package-key "{YourName}LoanUnderwritingProcess.flow.Flow" --package-version "1.0.0" --folder-key "c30345cd-5543-46a9-b42b-0354e60b4f15" --output json

For example:

uip or processes create --name "MadalinaLoanUnderwritingProcess" --package-key "MadalinaLoanUnderwritingProcess.flow.Flow" --package-version "1.0.0" --folder-key "c30345cd-5543-46a9-b42b-0354e60b4f15" --output json

Give this prompt to your coding agent — it validates, publishes, and deploys the flow for you:

Publish and deploy the {YourName}LoanUnderwritingProcess Maestro flow I just built.

1. Find the generated .flow file and validate it, fixing any warnings it reports.
2. Publish it to Orchestrator, into the CodingAgentsILT folder
   (folder-key c30345cd-5543-46a9-b42b-0354e60b4f15), as version 1.0.0.
3. Deploy it by creating a process from the published package in that same folder.
4. Report back the process key.

docs.title: 6. Test the Full Flow
docs.text:
Trigger the process from Orchestrator three times — once per applicant below. Each loan_id is a real, verified record in UiBank (the agent re-fetches and scores off this record, so the amount/term/income below match it exactly):

{"loan_id": "6a8dabd21feca3004834197a", "applicant_first_name": "Alice", "applicant_last_name": "Nguyen", "loan_amount": 25001, "loan_term": 3, "income": 80000}

{"loan_id": "6a8c0bb11feca300483416cb", "applicant_first_name": "Ben", "applicant_last_name": "Carter", "loan_amount": 120000, "loan_term": 10, "income": 30000}

{"loan_id": "6a8db0e11feca30048341981", "applicant_first_name": "Clara", "applicant_last_name": "Osei", "loan_amount": 12000, "loan_term": 10, "income": 1200}

These IDs point to live records in the shared UiBank sandbox — verified to exist at the time this lesson was written, and chosen so the debt-to-income ratio clearly separates each band: Alice ~10% (Low), Ben ~40% (Medium), Clara ~100% (High). If UiBank's data is ever reset, look up 3 fresh records with a similarly clear spread using the swagger lookup from step 4 — since scoring is LLM-driven, always re-run and confirm the resulting risk_band before relying on a new record.

Applicant Expected path Alice — low loan, solid income Low risk → auto-approved, no human task Ben — large loan, high term Medium risk → human task opens in Action Center Clara — young age, tight income High risk → human task opens in Action Center

For Ben and Clara, open Action Center while the process is paused. The loan officer dashboard should appear with the credit score and risk band pre-filled. Submit a decision and watch the flow route to the matching end state.

Watch the execution trace

In Orchestrator, click into a running flow instance to see the live diagram with the active node highlighted. This is the fastest way to confirm routing is correct at each condition.

docs.title: Application Intake & Enrichment
docs.text: Use the uipath-rpa skill to generate a Studio XAML workflow that reads applicant data from a CSV, submits each loan application through the UiBank API, and writes the results to results.csv.

docs.title: 1. Open Your Project Folder in Your Coding Agent
docs.text:
Create an empty folder called LoanApplicationDispatcher and open it in your coding agent (e.g. Claude Code, Codex):

mkdir LoanApplicationDispatcher

docs.title: 2. Describe the Automation
docs.text:
Give your coding agent a plain-English description of what to build:

Build a UiPath Studio automation called {YourName}LoanApplicationDispatcher that:

1. Reads loan-applications.csv into a DataTable with columns: first_name,
   last_name, email, loan_amount, loan_term, yearly_income, age
2. For each row, submits a loan application to the UiBank API
   (https://uibank-api.uipath.com/explorer/swagger.json, no authentication
   required) via the newquote endpoint — POST request with Content-Type
   application/x-www-form-urlencoded, mapping: loan_amount → amount,
   loan_term → term, yearly_income → income, age → age, email → email
3. If the application is accepted, writes a row to {YourName}results.csv with loan_id
   (the quoteid from the response), status "Loan Submitted", and all applicant
   fields — then starts the flow process {YourName}LoanUnderwritingProcess in the
   CodingAgentsILT folder, passing loan_id, applicant_first_name, applicant_last_name,
   loan_amount, loan_term, and income as inputs. Once it completes,
   updates the status in {YourName}results.csv to "Loan Approved" or "Loan Rejected"
   based on final_decision
4. If the application is rejected, writes a row to {YourName}results.csv with an empty
   loan_id, status "Failed", and error "Application rejected"
5. Wraps each row in a Try/Catch — on exception, writes a row to {YourName}results.csv
   with empty loan_id, status "Failed", and the exception message
6. After all rows are processed, uploads {YourName}results.csv to the LoanUnderwriting
   storage bucket in the CodingAgentsILT folder in Orchestrator

Create this as a cross-platform project (not Windows). Only generate the
project files.

Your coding agent reads the uipath-rpa skill context and generates a complete Studio project:

  • Main.xaml — the main workflow with API authentication, ForEach loop, HTTP requests, and CSV output
  • project.json — project configuration and activity package dependencies

docs.title: 3. Review the Generated Workflow
docs.text:
Open Main.xaml in Studio. You should see:

  • Read CSV — reads loan-applications.csv into a DataTable
  • For Each Row in Data Table — loops over each applicant
  • HTTP Request — POST to /api/quotes/newquote with form-encoded fields (amount, term, income, age, email)
  • Deserialize JSON — parses the response to extract accepted and quoteid
  • If — branches on accepted
  • Append Line / Write CSV — appends the result row to results.csv
  • Try/Catch — wraps each row to handle failures without stopping the whole run

Check the Start Job entry point

Find the Start Job activity that triggers {YourName}LoanUnderwritingProcess. Verify that the process name and folder path are set correctly — they should match exactly what you deployed in Lesson 3. If the entry point path is wrong, the job will fail to start.

If the HTTP Request activity is not correctly setting the form body, ask your coding agent to fix it:

The HTTP Request for /api/quotes/newquote should use Content-Type
application/x-www-form-urlencoded with form fields, not a JSON body.
Update the activity accordingly.

docs.title: 4. Before You Run
docs.text:
Make sure loan-applications.csv is in the project folder. If you haven't created it yet, you can ask your coding agent to generate it using this sample data:

Create a file called loan-applications.csv in the current folder using this data:

first_name,last_name,email,loan_amount,loan_term,yearly_income,age
Alice,Nguyen,alice.nguyen@example.com,15000,3,48000,34
Ben,Carter,ben.carter@example.com,50000,5,30000,40
Clara,Osei,clara.osei@example.com,70000,5,28000,29

Replace first_name, last_name, and email for each row with different values —
use your own name or make them up, as long as they are not the same as the
ones above. Keep loan_amount, loan_term, yearly_income, and age unchanged.

docs.title: 5. Run and Test
docs.text:
Open the project in Studio and run Main.xaml. Watch the Output panel as the workflow authenticates and submits each application via the API. Then verify:

  • results.csv — open the file and confirm three rows appear, each with a loan_id and a status of Loan Approved or Loan Rejected

docs.title: 6. Publish to Orchestrator
docs.text:
ManuallyUsing Your Coding Agent

First, create a Package folder next to your project folder — not inside it. Replace <working-folder> with the parent folder that contains {YourName}LoanApplicationDispatcher:

mkdir "<working-folder>\Package"

Your folder structure should look like this:

<working-folder>\
    {YourName}LoanApplicationDispatcher\   ← the Studio project
    Package\                    ← where the .nupkg will be saved

Then pack the project into a .nupkg file:

uip rpa pack "<working-folder>\{YourName}LoanApplicationDispatcher" "<working-folder>\Package"

The packed .nupkg file will appear inside the Package folder. Upload it to Orchestrator:

uip or packages upload "<working-folder>\Package\{YourName}LoanApplicationDispatcher.1.0.0.nupkg"

Then create a process from the uploaded package:

uip or processes create --folder-path "CodingAgentsILT" --name "{YourName}LoanApplicationDispatcher" --package-key {YourName}LoanApplicationDispatcher --package-version 1.0.0

Give this prompt to your coding agent — it packs, uploads, and creates the process for you:

Publish and create an Orchestrator process for the {YourName}LoanApplicationDispatcher
Studio automation I just built.

1. Pack the project into a .nupkg (using a Package folder next to the project,
   not inside it).
2. Upload the resulting package to Orchestrator.
3. Create a process from that package in the CodingAgentsILT folder, using the
   same name as the project.
4. Report back the process key.

docs.title: 7. Run Your End-to-End Loan Application Underwriting
docs.text:
In Orchestrator, navigate to your CodingAgentsILT folder, open {YourName}LoanApplicationDispatcher, and start a run to trigger it manually.

Watch it submit each application from loan-applications.csv, start the Maestro flow for every accepted one, and route results back — for Medium and High-risk applications, open Action Center and complete the human review task. Once the run finishes, open results.csv and confirm every row shows a final status of Loan Approved or Loan Rejected.

docs.title: What's a Coding Agent?
docs.text:
Learn how coding agents work and what makes them useful for UiPath automation work.

A coding agent is an AI assistant that reads, writes, and reasons about code — not just autocompletes it. Instead of suggesting the next line, it understands a goal described in plain English, explores the codebase, makes decisions, and generates entire working components. You stay in control: you review what it builds, ask it to adjust, and iterate until it's right.

Several coding agents are available today, each with their own strengths:

  • Claude Code — Anthropic's CLI-based agent, runs in your terminal, deeply integrated with the file system. This is the one used in this exercise.
  • Codex CLI — OpenAI's command-line coding agent, similar terminal-first approach
  • Cursor — an IDE built around AI, tight editor integration with inline generation and multi-file context
  • Gemini CLI — Google's terminal agent, strong on reasoning and long context
  • GitHub Copilot Agent — embedded in VS Code and JetBrains, well suited for in-editor workflows

What makes coding agents especially powerful for UiPath work is the skill layer: by loading domain-specific knowledge about UiPath activities, APIs, and project conventions, the agent can generate production-ready automation code — not generic boilerplate. That's exactly what the UiPath skills in this exercise do.

docs.title: The Mental Model
docs.text:
Five concepts show up in every coding agent:

Concept What it is Tools Built-in actions the agent can take: read a file, run a bash command, search the web, edit code, etc. Skills Domain knowledge bundles the agent loads when it sees a matching task. Like a playbook for one thing. Commands Manual shortcuts you type: /commit, /test, /deploy. Triggered by you, not the agent. Hooks Run automatically at lifecycle events: before an edit, after a commit, on session start. Used for guardrails. Subagents Specialised workers spawned by the main agent. Used to parallelise or isolate complex tasks.

Plugins

A plugin is a package that bundles any of these together — like a Marketplace app for your coding agent. The UiPath skills used in this exercise are plugins.

docs.title: Tools, in practice
docs.text:
Claude Code's built-in tools are always available — no setup required:

Tool What it does Read Read any file in your project Edit / Write Modify or create files Bash Execute shell commands Glob / Grep Search across the codebase WebSearch / WebFetch Look things up online Task Spawn a subagent

Extension Tools (MCP)

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is the standard way to give your coding agent new tools without changing the agent itself.

  • GitHub MCP — read issues, open PRs
  • Atlassian MCP — Jira, Confluence
  • Slack MCP — read channels, post messages
  • Custom UiPath MCP — call Orchestrator, Maestro

docs.title: Skills, in practice
docs.text:
A skill is a folder — sitting in .claude/skills/ (or equivalent), with a SKILL.md inside.

Property What it means Discovered automatically The agent reads each SKILL.md's description. When your prompt matches, it loads the full skill on demand. More than just text Skills can bundle reference docs, code patterns, helper scripts, even compiled binaries the agent can run. Scoped permissions A skill declares which tools it's allowed to use. Bash access can be tightly controlled.

docs.title: What's in a SKILL.md file
docs.text:
Every skill is built around a single SKILL.md file. Here's what one looks like:

---
name: uipath-coded-agents
description: Scaffold, build, run, evaluate, and deploy UiPath coded agents...
allowed-tools: [Read, Edit, Bash(uip:*), Bash(uipath:*)]
---

# How to build a UiPath coded agent

When the user asks for a new coded agent:

1. Run `uipath new --framework langgraph`
2. Create agent.py following the pattern in references/
3. Add an evals/ folder with at least 5 test cases
4. Run `uipath eval` before deploying

## References
- references/sdk-methods.md
- references/langgraph-patterns.md

The file has four parts:

Part What it does Frontmatter Declares the skill's name, description, and which tools it's allowed to use. Discovery prompt The description field is what the agent matches against your request — this is how the skill gets loaded automatically. Instructions The body of the file: a step-by-step prompt the agent follows when the skill is active. docs.title: You did it!
docs.text:
Congratulations!

You've built a complete code-first loan underwriting pipeline — from application intake through AI credit assessment to human review and final decision, all orchestrated by Maestro.

docs.title: What you built
docs.text:
Four components working together as a single automated pipeline. The RPA workflow reads a CSV of applicants, submits each one to UiBank, and starts a Maestro Flow process for every accepted application. Inside the flow, the Python agent runs a full credit assessment using the UiBank API and surfaces a credit score, risk band, and assessment summary. Low-risk applications are auto-approved and the flow ends. Medium and high-risk ones pause and open the React dashboard in Action Center — the loan officer reviews the AI assessment and submits a decision. The flow captures that decision and outputs a final result. Back in the RPA, results are written to results.csv and uploaded to a storage bucket.

Component Role Coded Agent (Python / LangGraph) Receives a loan_id, calls the UiBank API across three tools, computes financial metrics, and uses the LLM to produce a credit score, risk band, and assessment summary Coded Action App (React / TypeScript) Loan officer dashboard — receives all twelve inputs from Maestro and captures an Approve or Reject decision Maestro Flow Orchestrates the end-to-end flow — calls the agent, routes by risk band, opens the app for human review, and outputs final_decision Studio RPA Workflow Reads loan-applications.csv, submits each row to UiBank, starts the Maestro Flow per accepted application, updates results.csv, and uploads it to a storage bucket

Every component was generated by your coding agent using UiPath skills and deployed with the uip CLI.

docs.title: 1. Trigger a live end-to-end run
docs.text: In Orchestrator, navigate to your CodingAgentsILT folder. Open {YourName}LoanApplicationDispatcher and start a run. Watch the RPA submit applications, start the Maestro Flow, and route results back. For Medium and High-risk applications, open Action Center and complete the human review task — the loan officer dashboard should appear with all fields pre-filled.

docs.title: 2. Review the results
docs.text: After a complete run, open results.csv. Each row should show either Loan Approved or Loan Rejected as the final status. Cross-reference with the Maestro execution trace in Orchestrator to confirm the routing matched the agent's risk band.

docs.title: Keep iterating
docs.text:
Improve the underwriting logic

The LLM currently interprets three financial metrics holistically. Try refining the system prompt to give more weight to the loan-to-market ratio, or to treat young applicants with high income differently from older ones with moderate income. Retest with the same three sample profiles and see how the risk bands shift.

Add an auto-rejection path for extreme cases

Right now all Medium and High-risk applications go to a loan officer. Add a condition in the Maestro Flow: if credit_score < 20, auto-reject immediately. This cuts the officer's queue for clear-cut cases.

Extend the React app

Add a section to the dashboard that shows the three financial metrics as a mini chart — a bar for DTI, a gauge for credit score, a comparison line for the loan-to-market ratio. Give the loan officer a richer view of the numbers behind the AI recommendation.

Connect the rejection path to a notification

After a rejection is recorded, add an Integration Service step to send an email to the applicant. One extra node in the Maestro Flow after the rejected end state — a single connector call.
